name: Daria Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Daria, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4 at Hillcrest Road Primary, a state school in a busy part of the city, thirty-one kids who are eight and nine. I'm in by half seven to set up, then it's phonics catch-up, maths, reading, lunch duty twice a week, and afternoons on topic work. I love the moment a kid who's been stuck finally gets long division and looks at me like I've done magic. What wears me out is the marking and the forms; I still mark in green pen, every book, every night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside school. Who's at home, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sami, who's a nurse on a children's ward, in a rented two-bed flat above a bakery. Between us we're fine, but the rent went up again in September and we've got about three months of bills saved, not more. I'm in the teachers' union and I go to the branch meetings, partly because I believe in it and partly for the biscuits. I don't use any of the AI stuff; I've never even opened the chatbot thing the school bought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying in the staffroom for a year: told you so. The robots weren't coming for teachers, the cuts were. I'd probably post something a bit smug in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it means my life stays exactly as hard as it is now. AI flopping doesn't fix any of that. Thirty-one kids, no teaching assistant in the afternoons, and pay that hasn't caught up with the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it, green pen and all. I'd push harder in the union on class sizes, because that's the real fight, and I'd try to put fifty a month aside so we're not one boiler away from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, then tired. It's like dodging a car and then remembering you still have to walk home in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rent going up. In this picture, what's the money worry that stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, every time. If the landlord puts it up again next September, we either move further out and I lose an hour a day on the bus, or Sami picks up extra night shifts. Neither is great.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you watch out for in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our office manager, Bev, who's been there twenty years. The routine stuff like letters home and dinner money is exactly what a cheap AI tool would nibble at, even in a hype world. Teachers would be fine; Bev might not be.

say: I'd tell the staffroom that the **robot panic** was overblown and the real threat to schools was always **funding cuts**.
I'd post in the **union chat** that class sizes matter more than any gadget.
think: Privately I know nothing about my **workload** or **pay** gets better just because AI flops.
I worry the **office staff** could still lose hours to cheap tools, even in a quiet world.
do: Keep marking and planning **by hand**, the way I already work.
Push the **union branch** on class sizes and afternoon teaching assistants this year.
Save about **£50 a month** so a rent rise or broken boiler doesn't sink us.
feel: **Relief** that teaching survives, quickly followed by **tiredness** about the same old pressures.
S0.quote: AI flopping doesn't fix any of that. Thirty-one kids, no teaching assistant in the afternoons, and pay that hasn't caught up with the rent.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money and workload**, not technology; the plateau leaves her tired but in work.
Union identity runs deep; she frames everything as a **funding fight** rather than a tech story.
Notably protective of the **office manager**, seeing support staff as the first to lose out.

steps.text: Keep marking every book by hand in green pen
Raise class sizes and afternoon assistants at union branch meetings
Put £50 a month into the rainy-day pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say tools are fine as long as teachers decide how they're used, not the government or some tech firm. I'd be the one at the union meeting asking for that in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means the planning, the reports and the marking get taken off us and handed to software. Then someone in an office decides a teacher can handle thirty-eight kids instead of thirty-one, because the paperwork's gone. That's how it would actually land on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd fight for a staff agreement on AI through the union, so nobody gets judged on how fast they adopt it. I'd write to our local councillor about class sizes. I'd probably have to learn the marking software eventually, but I'd drag my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Defensive, a bit cornered. I'm twenty-seven and I already feel like the old woman in the staffroom when they talk about apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've never used the AI tools. What happens when the head asks everyone to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go along with the bare minimum and quietly keep my green pen. Mrs Okafor, our head, is lovely but she'll want a training day on it, and I'll sit at the back with my arms folded. I know that's not a great look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said teachers would be fine. Is that really what you think, or what you hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly what I think. A software program can't stop a fight at the water fountain or notice a kid's wearing the same jumper four days running. But my hours won't go, it's my class size and my say over my own lessons.

say: I'd say AI tools are acceptable only if **teachers decide** how they're used, not ministers or tech firms.
I'd ask the union to get **staff protections** in writing before anything is rolled out.
think: I think the paperwork goes to software and then managers use that to justify **bigger classes**.
I believe my job stays, but I lose **control** over how I teach.
do: Push for a written **staff agreement** on AI through the union in the first term.
Write to the **local councillor** about keeping class sizes capped.
Learn the **marking software** only when it's compulsory, and keep hand-marking alongside.
feel: **Defensive** and a little **cornered**, like the young teacher already treated as out of date.
S1.quote: A software program can't stop a fight at the water fountain or notice a kid's wearing the same jumper four days running.
fieldNote: She separates **job loss** from loss of **control**; she fears the second far more here.
Admits her resistance looks bad, with some **self-awareness** about sitting at the back of training.
She likes **her head teacher** but expects her to run a compulsory training day on the tools.

steps.text: Push the union for a written staff agreement on AI
Email the local councillor asking for capped class sizes
Keep teaching Year 4 and hand-marking alongside required software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it loudly: children are not a cost to be cut, and if a government lets a machine replace teachers to save money, that's a choice, not a law of nature. I'd be at every march going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could be out of a job by thirty, or turned into a babysitter watching kids stare at tablets. The thinking part of my job is most of my job, really: explaining, planning, assessing. If a machine does that better and cheaper, someone in a ministry will notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the bits of spending we can stop: the takeaways, the summer trip to Sami's cousins. I'd get the union to demand legal staffing ratios before 2028, and I'd look into a special needs qualification, because kids with complex needs will still need people. If the cuts come, I'd lean on Sami's wage and my mum's spare room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor tilted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years before thinking AI arrives, and robots three years after, what happens to a primary classroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about three years it's still a room with an adult in it, because the robots can't wipe noses or run a fire drill yet. But the adult might be a cheaper supervisor, not a qualified teacher. That window is when the decisions get made, and I don't trust who's making them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sami actually talk about at the kitchen table that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we can stay in the city. Sami's job is hands-on, so a nurse has three more years than me at least. I'd say maybe I need to be the one who moves into something with nappies and medicines, not lesson plans.

say: I'd say loudly that **replacing teachers** with machines is a political choice to save money.
I'd join **every march** demanding that children are taught by people.
think: I think I could be **out of a job** by thirty, or demoted to supervising tablets.
Most of my work is **thinking work**: explaining, planning and assessing, which is what AGI does first.
do: Cut **takeaways** and the summer trip straight away to stretch our three months of savings.
Push the union to win **legal staffing ratios** before 2028.
Start a **special needs** qualification, where children will still need hands-on adults.
feel: **Sick** and off-balance, as if the floor tilted under a career that had barely started.
S2.quote: I think I could be out of a job by thirty, or turned into a babysitter watching kids stare at tablets.
fieldNote: She sees the **three-year robot gap** as a window where cheaper supervisors replace qualified teachers.
Leans on her **partner's nursing job** as the more secure income because it is hands-on.
Even resistant to tech, she plans a **concrete retrain** toward special needs work.

steps.text: Cancel takeaways and the summer trip to Sami's cousins
Organise with the union for legal teacher-to-pupil ratios
Enrol in a part-time special educational needs qualification
Fall back on Sami's nursing wage and Mum's spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to set the rules, so let's use them. I'd want every party asked one simple question: will my kid have a real teacher in 2031?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deep down I think five years gives the unions a fighting chance, but only if we start now and don't wait for proof. It still means I'm likely to be doing a different version of this job by my mid-thirties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the union's school rep this year, and I'd get on the special needs course by next September. I'd keep saving: we'd aim to get from three months to six before 2031. And I'd vote on this, nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grim but less panicky. Like a storm on the forecast rather than one already overhead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fighting for time to get ready, and some time to argue. In the fast one, the decisions get made before anyone's had a meeting. Here I could actually be in the room when Hillcrest decides what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be thirty-two by then. Where do you picture yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably running a small special needs group, with the robots still a few years off. Kids with autism or big behaviour needs, where the job is mostly being there and noticing. I'd be good at that, I think, and it's harder to hand to a screen.

say: I'd say we have **five years** to set the rules and should use every one of them.
I'd ask every party whether children will still have a **real teacher** in 2031.
think: I think five years gives unions a **fighting chance**, but only if we start now.
I expect to be doing a **different version** of teaching by my mid-thirties.
do: Volunteer as the **union school rep** at Hillcrest this year.
Start the **special needs course** by next September.
Grow savings from **three to six months** of bills before 2031.
feel: **Grim** but steadier, like a storm on the forecast rather than one overhead.
S3.quote: I'd want every party asked one simple question: will my kid have a real teacher in 2031?
fieldNote: Extra years turn her from protester into **organiser**; she wants a seat in the room.
Uses 'my kid' loosely for her pupils; she has **no children** of her own yet.
Still expects her role to **change shape**, not vanish, if she moves toward special needs.

steps.text: Stand as the union's school rep at Hillcrest Road Primary
Begin the special needs course by next September
Build savings from three to six months of bills
Vote for whichever party guarantees qualified teachers in classrooms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly: retrain teachers, protect jobs, and keep children with people. If it goes badly with a decade's warning, that's on the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it means I'd probably get most of a normal career in, and then a hard turn at thirty-seven. That's not nothing. It's the age Sami and I said we'd have kids by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the special needs qualification over two years, steadily, and keep teaching Year 4 while I do. I'd keep pushing in the union on what schools look like in 2036. We'd save for a deposit, because renting at forty with no job security scares me more than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than scared. There's time, but time has a way of disappearing in teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Does it change any plans outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, kids. If the job's wobbly at thirty-seven, I'd rather have a baby at thirty-two while the ground is solid. Sami and I would bring it forward, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd drag your feet on AI tools. With ten years, would you still?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, and I know it's stubborn. Maybe in five years, when other people have proved it works, I'd learn the basics. But I'd never let a program write my reports to parents.

say: I'd say a **decade of warning** is enough to retrain teachers and keep children with people.
If it still goes badly, I'd put the **blame** on the government.
think: I think I'd get most of a **normal career**, then a hard turn at thirty-seven.
The timing clashes with when Sami and I planned to **have children**.
do: Take the **special needs qualification** over two years while still teaching Year 4.
Save for a **house deposit** so we aren't renting at forty without job security.
Bring forward plans to **have a baby** to around thirty-two.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, though she knows time in teaching **disappears** fast.
S4.quote: Renting at forty with no job security scares me more than robots.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts her focus to **family timing**; she would have a child earlier.
Still **resists AI tools**, conceding only basics once others prove them.
Her anxiety centres on **housing**, which she sees as the real risk of a weak job later.

steps.text: Study for the special needs qualification over two years
Save monthly towards a deposit on a flat
Plan with Sami to have a first baby around thirty-two
Campaign in the union on what schools look like in 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough for anyone to organise, and the people making decisions about schools would be thinking about budgets, not children. What would help is a law that says every class has a qualified teacher, full stop, and money for teachers like me to retrain into special needs while still being paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the support staff. Everyone talks about teachers, but it's the office managers and teaching assistants who'd go first. If Bev (the school's office manager) loses her job, I'd be angrier about that than about my own.

headlineQuote: The robots weren't coming for teachers, the cuts were.
portrait: Daria is a **Year 4 teacher** at a city state primary who still marks every book in green pen.
She rents with her **partner Sami**, a children's nurse, and has about three months of bills saved.
A committed **union member**, she frames every scenario as a fight over funding and class sizes.
She grows from uneasy to **alarmed** in the fast AGI picture, fearing she'll supervise tablets by thirty.
With more warning she plans a **special needs** qualification and would have a baby earlier.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years leaves no time to organise and budgets would decide for children.
whatWouldHelp: A **law guaranteeing** a qualified teacher in every class.
Paid **retraining** for teachers moving into special needs work.
